nameStory: The greenhouse frog earned its name from its habit of taking up residence in warm, humid greenhouses where it finds ideal living conditions. These tiny tropical frogs often hitchhike to new locations in potted plants and garden supplies, making greenhouses their perfect new home away from home.
description: The greenhouse frog is a tiny tropical amphibian, roughly the size of your thumbnail, that's native to Cuba and the Caribbean but has been introduced to parts of North America. These diminutive frogs have smooth, moist skin and typically measure less than an inch long when fully grown. They're part of the rain frog family, which means they skip the tadpole stage entirely and develop directly from eggs into miniature frogs. In New England, they're extremely rare visitors, likely arriving accidentally in plant shipments.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Exceptionally tiny, typically under an inch long - about the size of your thumbnail or a large raisin

idTips.label: Skin
idTips.description: Smooth, moist skin that feels slightly sticky to the touch, lacking the bumpy texture of toads

idTips.label: Color/Pattern
idTips.description: Usually brown to reddish-brown with darker markings, sometimes with a lighter stripe down the back

idTips.label: Call
idTips.description: High-pitched chirping or peeping sound, often described as cricket-like or bird-like rather than a typical frog croak

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Relatively large, prominent eyes compared to body size, with horizontal pupils

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found around human structures, particularly in warm, humid areas like greenhouses, basements, or under potted plants

habitat: In New England, greenhouse frogs would most likely be found in heated greenhouses, conservatories, or indoor plant collections where temperatures and humidity remain tropical year-round. They prefer hiding under pots, in soil, or among leaf litter in these artificial environments. Since they cannot survive New England winters outdoors, any sightings would be limited to heated indoor spaces.

seasonality.spring: Any activity would be limited to heated indoor spaces. May be more active as greenhouse temperatures rise with longer daylight hours.
seasonality.summer: Most likely time for accidental introductions through plant shipments. Could potentially survive briefly outdoors in very warm weather but unlikely to establish populations.
seasonality.fall: Activity would decline except in consistently heated indoor environments as outdoor temperatures drop below their tolerance.
seasonality.winter: Completely dependent on heated indoor spaces for survival. Any outdoor populations would not survive New England's freezing temperatures.

funFact: Greenhouse frogs never go through a tadpole stage - they hatch directly from their eggs as tiny, fully-formed frogs, making them one of the few amphibians that never need water to reproduce!
confusionNotes: Their tiny size makes them most likely to be confused with very young native frogs, but greenhouse frogs can be distinguished by their preference for indoor habitats and their direct development (no tadpole stage). Remember: if you find a thumbnail-sized frog in your greenhouse or basement, it's probably not a baby - it's a full-grown greenhouse frog!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'frog,' greenhouse frogs belong to a completely different family (rain frogs) than most familiar North American frogs. They're considered an invasive species when they establish populations outside their native range, though they're not known to survive outdoors in New England's climate.
compareHints: Since no other rain frogs occur in New England, greenhouse frogs are most similar to young spring peepers in size. However, greenhouse frogs lack the distinctive X-pattern on their back that peepers have, prefer indoor habitats rather than outdoor breeding pools, and have a more cricket-like call rather than the clear peeping of spring peepers. Unlike peepers, they also develop directly from eggs without a tadpole stage.
